title: 懸念強まる超長期国債　「物価高補正予算」4兆円に身構える海外勢
extracted_text:
国内債券市場でインフレや財政拡張への懸念が晴れない。とりわけ償還期間が10年を超える超長期国債の利回り上昇が目立つ。中東情勢の混迷が続くなか、防衛関連や経済対策に伴う財政悪化が改めて意識されている。

2022年度の岸田文雄政権（当時）が物価高対策で投じた4兆円が補正予算の目安とされ、その規模次第で振れ幅が大きくなりそうだ。

「（積極財政と金融緩和を組み合わせた）リフレ志向の政策を重視しつつ、中東混迷に伴う影響への対応を進めている点を踏まえると、日本の財政見通しを巡る懸念は強い」。米有力債券投資会社、ダブルライン・キャピタルでポートフォリオ・マネジャーを務めるビル・キャンベル氏はこうみる。同氏の見方を裏付けるかのように、足元では日本国債から距離を置く動きが広がる。

30日の債券市場では新発40年物国債利回りが前営業日比0.115%高い3.98%をつけた。節目の4%をつけていた3月末以来の高さで、1月につけた過去最高の4.2%台からも遠くない。新発30年債利回りも一時3.74%と同0.1%上昇した。超長期債は短中期債に比べて財政懸念をより織り込むとされる。

売りの根底にあるのが原油高騰に起因するインフレ圧力だ。エネルギー輸送の要衝であるホルムズ海峡の事実上の封鎖で、物価を巡る環境は様変わりした。広範な領域に物価高が波及し国民生活の重荷になるなか、ガソリン補助金などの経済対策が膨らむとの見方がもっぱらだ。

こうしたなか、プロが注目するのが30年債と2年債の利回り差（複利ベース）だ。市場における財政懸念の度合いを端的に示すとされ、3月以降に再び上昇している。30日には1月下旬以来およそ3カ月ぶりに2.3%台後半に上昇した。

3月以降は日銀が4月の金融政策決定会合で利上げに動くとの観測が高まっていた時期と重なる。ただ、それ以上に財政懸念を通じた超長期債への売り圧力が強まってきた証左が、この金利差拡大から読み取れる。

高市早苗首相は現時点で、中東情勢の緊迫化や原油価格高騰の対策を巡り「補正予算の編成が必要な状況とは考えていない」と明言している。ただ、市場では「ここまで原油価格が上がると、財政リスクを意識せざるを得ない」（国内証券の債券ディーラー）といった見方が散見される。

過去の実績で参考になりそうなのが、同じく原油高に伴う物価高対応に動いた22年度だ。

当時は22年度第1次補正予算では歳出の規模が約2.7兆円となった。大和証券の浜田浩史シニアエコノミストの試算によると、第2次補正予算の成立までに岸田政権が原油高・物価高対策に投じた金額は4.1兆円規模に上るという。今回も同等の水準が一つの参考になり得る。

ただ、当時は新型コロナウイルス禍への対応も重なっていたため、5兆円程度の予備費が活用できた。今回は1兆円程度と規模に違いがある。浜田氏は「災害対策なども考慮すれば、物価高対応で使える分はせいぜい5000億円程度ではないか」とみる。

ホルムズ海峡を巡る情勢が長引けば、その分こうした予算規模は膨らむことになる。仮に補正予算の検討が進む場合、5〜6月にかけてのヘッドライン（ニュースの見出し）に債券市場は振らされやすくなる。

海外勢はこれまで安定的に日本の超長期債に買いを入れてきた。ただ、高市政権の「責任ある積極財政」に対して懐疑的な声も聞かれ始めた。

シンガポールのヘッジファンド、モジュラーアセットマネジメントの最高投資責任者（CIO）、ジミー・リム氏は「原油ショックや金融正常化が迫るなか、積極的な財政支出はバランスの取れないものとなりかねない」と話す。「財政と金融の方針が乖離（かいり）すれば『債券自警団』が戻り、超長期ゾーンの落ち着きは失われかねない」

ダブルラインのキャンベル氏も、ガソリン補助金や消費税減税といった政策の組み合わせに加え、追加的な歳出を相殺できるだけの「信頼できる財源策が示されていない点が超長期債のタームプレミアム（上乗せ金利）の主因になっている」と指摘。長期や超長期ゾーンの日本国債はアンダーウエート（売り）姿勢を継続しているという。

発足時と比べて金融市場との対話姿勢を示すようになった高市政権。もっとも具体的な政策運営やその発信をひとたび誤れば、中東発でインフレの波が押し寄せるなか、市場のボラティリティー（変動率）が過度に高まり経済全体を揺さぶる恐れがある。

（生田弦己）

translated_text:
Concerns over inflation and fiscal expansion remain unresolved in the domestic bond market. Notably, the rise in yields on ultra-long-term government bonds with maturities exceeding 10 years is particularly pronounced. Amid continued chaos in the Middle East, the worsening of fiscal conditions due to defense-related and economic measures is once again being brought into focus.

The 4 trillion yen that the Kishida administration invested in FY2022 for price increase measures is being used as a benchmark for the supplementary budget, and fluctuations are expected to widen depending on the scale.

"Given that Japan is prioritizing reflationist policies combining active fiscal spending with monetary easing while responding to the impact of Middle East turmoil, concerns about Japan's fiscal outlook are strong." This is how Bill Campbell, portfolio manager at U.S. major bond investment firm DoubleLine Capital, sees it. As if to substantiate his view, moves to distance from Japanese government bonds are spreading.

In the bond market on the 30th, the yield on newly issued 40-year government bonds rose 0.115 percentage points from the previous business day to 3.98%. This is the highest level since the 4% threshold was reached at the end of March, and not far from the record high of around 4.2% hit in January. The yield on newly issued 30-year bonds also rose 0.1 percentage points to 3.74% at one point. Ultra-long-term bonds are said to incorporate fiscal concerns more than short- to medium-term bonds.

At the root of the selling is inflationary pressure stemming from surging oil prices. With the effective blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for energy transport, the environment surrounding prices has changed dramatically. With price hikes spreading across a wide area and burdening citizens' lives, there is a prevailing view that economic measures such as gasoline subsidies will expand.

Amid this, what professionals are watching is the yield spread between 30-year and 2-year bonds (on a compound basis). It is considered a straightforward indicator of the degree of fiscal concerns in the market, and has been rising again since March. On the 30th, it rose to the high 2.3% range for the first time since late January, roughly three months later.

Since March, this coincides with the period when market expectations were rising that the Bank of Japan would raise interest rates at its April monetary policy decision meeting. However, evidence that selling pressure on ultra-long-term bonds has intensified beyond that, through fiscal concerns, can be read from this widening yield spread.

Prime Minister Maebashi has explicitly stated that at the current moment, she does not believe the situation requires preparing a supplementary budget regarding measures against the Middle East situation escalation or surging oil prices. However, in the market, views such as "once oil prices rise this much, we cannot help but be aware of fiscal risks" (from a bond trader at a domestic securities firm) can be seen here and there.

What may serve as a reference from past performance is FY2022, when measures were taken in response to price hikes driven by surging oil prices.

At that time, the first supplementary budget for FY2022 had expenditures of around 2.7 trillion yen. According to calculations by Hiroshi Hamada, senior economist at Daiwa Securities, the amount the Kishida administration invested in oil price and price hike measures by the time the second supplementary budget was enacted reached around 4.1 trillion yen. This time as well, a similar level could serve as one reference.

However, at that time, responses to the COVID-19 pandemic were also overlapping, so reserve funds of around 5 trillion yen could be utilized. This time, the scale is different, at around 1 trillion yen. Hamada observes, "Considering disaster response and other measures, the portion that can be used for price hike应对 would be at most around 500 billion yen, perhaps."

If the situation regarding the Strait of Hormuz drags on, budget sizes will expand accordingly. If consideration of a supplementary budget advances, the bond market will become more susceptible to headlines around May-June.

Foreign investors have consistently bought Japan's ultra-long-term bonds stably until now. However, skepticism is also beginning to be heard regarding the Maebashi administration's "responsible active fiscal policy."

Jimmy Lim, Chief Investment Officer at Singapore hedge fund Modular Asset Management, says, "Active fiscal spending may become unbalanced amid oil shocks and nearing financial normalization." He adds, "If fiscal and monetary policies diverge, the 'bond vigilantes' may return, and the stability of the ultra-long-term zone could be lost."

Campbell at DoubleLine also points out that the lack of credible financing measures to offset additional expenditures, combined with policies like gasoline subsidies or consumption tax cuts, is the main cause of the term premium on ultra-long-term bonds. The firm continues to maintain an underweight position on Japanese government bonds in the long-term and ultra-long-term zones.

Compared to when it was established, the Maebashi administration has shown a more dialogical stance with financial markets. However, if specific policy management or its communication is even once mistaken, amid inflation waves arriving from the Middle East, market volatility could excessively rise and potentially shake the entire economy.

(Ikuta Sumitomo)
